title: Construction and functoriality of the unipotent exponential
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of characteristic zero. Let $G$ be an affine $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] admitting a closed group-scheme immersion $i:G\hookrightarrow U_n$ for some $n\geq1$ [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Here $U_n(R)$ is the upper unitriangular subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ [def-sc-general-linear-group] for each commutative $k$-algebra $R$. Put $\mathfrak g=T_{G/k,e}$ [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space, def-sc-dual-numbers]. Its image under $\mathrm di$ is the vector space of strictly upper triangular matrices $X$ such that $I+\epsilon X\in G(k[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$. For any $R$, the same linear equations identify $R\otimes_k\mathfrak g$ with the matrices $X$ such that $I+\epsilon X\in G(R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The space $\mathfrak g$ is finite-dimensional over $k$. Write $\mathfrak g_a$ for its additive vector scheme: after a basis of size $d$ is chosen it is $\operatorname{Spec}k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$ with coordinatewise addition [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-sc-gm-ga], representing $R\mapsto R\otimes_k\mathfrak g$. There exists a $k$-scheme morphism $\exp_G:\mathfrak g_a\to G$, natural on $R$-points, characterized by
$$i_R(\exp_G(X))=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\frac{(\mathrm di_R(X))^r}{r!}.$$
It is independent of the unitriangular embedding. For another such group $H$ and any group-scheme homomorphism $f:G\to H$, its tangent map satisfies
$$f_R(\exp_G(X))=\exp_H((1\otimes\mathrm df)(X)).$$
If $X,Y\in R\otimes_k\mathfrak g$ have commuting matrix images, then
$$\exp_G(X+Y)=\exp_G(X)\exp_G(Y).$$
No invertibility of $\exp_G$ is asserted.

source.place: 14.28 and 14.31, printed pp.287--289: finite exponential, construction using Theorem 9.2, formula (93), and the naturality square immediately before Proposition 14.32. Tangent coordinates are as in 10.8 and 10.14.

proof.text: Write the coordinates of $U_n$ as $z_{ij}=u_{ij}$ for $i<j$, so its identity is $z=0$. By the affine description of a closed immersion, $G=\operatorname{Spec}(k[z_{ij}]/J)$, with $p(0)=0$ for $p\in J$. Substitution $z_{ij}=\epsilon x_{ij}$ gives $p(\epsilon x)=\epsilon\ell_p(x)$, where $\ell_p$ is the linear part of $p$. Thus the dual-number description of the tangent space is exactly the common kernel of these $k$-linear forms on $k^{n(n-1)/2}$. Choose a basis of their span (a subspace of a finite-dimensional dual space) and row-reduce its finite coefficient matrix over $k$. Its nonzero pivots remain units in every $k$-algebra $R$, and the same free-variable basis describes its kernel over $R$. This identifies the kernel with $R\otimes_k\mathfrak g$, including the zero algebra. In particular $\mathfrak g$ has finite dimension $d$. In strictly upper triangular matrices, every summand of an entry of a product of $n$ factors needs a strictly increasing chain of $n+1$ indices in $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, so the product is zero.

source.place: 10.7--10.8, printed pp.188--189, dual-number matrix calculation; linear equations and coefficient-algebra version written out.

proof.text: Every finite-dimensional rational representation $V$ of $G$ has a flag with one-dimensional trivial quotients. Here is the dimension induction: it is empty for $V=0$; for $V\ne0$, choose a basis and apply [lem-sfb-unitriangular-subgroup-rational-fixed-vector] to obtain a fixed nonzero vector $v$. The line $kv$ is a rational submodule. In the coaction description [lem-sfb-rational-representation-comodule-dictionary], its coaction is $v\mapsto v\otimes1$, so the coaction descends to $V/kv$; the two coaction identities descend as well. Apply the induction hypothesis to this space of dimension $\dim(V)-1$ and take inverse images of its flag, starting with $kv$. A basis adapted to the resulting flag makes every $r_{V,A}(g)$ upper unitriangular for every coefficient algebra $A$. Evaluate it on the tangent point $I+\epsilon\,\mathrm di_R(X)\in G(R[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2)$ from step 1. Its action is $1+\epsilon D_V(X)$ with $D_V(X)=(1\otimes\mathrm dr_V)(X)$. Indeed, by [def-weil-affine-spectrum] the matrix entries of $r_V-1$ are elements of $k[z_{ij}]/J$ vanishing at $z=0$; substituting $z=\epsilon\,\mathrm di_R(X)$ as in step 1 leaves $\epsilon$ times their linear parts evaluated at $\mathrm di_R(X)$. This is $R$-linear in $X$, compatible with every $k$-algebra map $R\to S$, and for $R=k$ it is $\mathrm dr_V$ by the composition definition of the tangent map. Moreover $D_V(X)$ is strictly upper triangular in that basis. Consequently $D_V(X)^{\dim V}=0$ when $V\ne0$; on the zero space use the bound $1$.

source.place: 14.3 and 14.5, printed pp.280--281; 14.31, printed p.288, nilpotence of every differential representation.

proof.text:
Set $\lambda_V(X)=E_{\operatorname{End}_R(V_R)}(D_V(X))$, using [lem-sfb-nilpotent-exponential-identities] and the bounds in step 2. The dual-number definition of the differential and the tensor representation formula give
$$D_{V\otimes W}(X)=D_V(X)\otimes1+1\otimes D_W(X).$$
Indeed, expand $(1+\epsilon D_V)\otimes(1+\epsilon D_W)$ and discard $\epsilon^2$. On the trivial representation $k$, the differential is zero. For an equivariant map $u:V\to W$, evaluating equivariance on the same tangent point gives $D_W(X)u_R=u_RD_V(X)$. Multiplying repeatedly gives $D_W(X)^ju_R=u_RD_V(X)^j$ for all $j$. Taking any common nilpotence bound in the finite sums therefore gives $\lambda_W(X)u_R=u_R\lambda_V(X)$, and $\lambda_k(X)=1$.

source.place: 14.31 (b),(c), printed p.288, with the differential tensor formula obtained by expansion over dual numbers.

proof.text:
Put $P=D_V(X)\otimes1$ and $Q=1\otimes D_W(X)$ on $V_R\otimes_RW_R$. These commute: on $v\otimes w$, both composites give $D_V(X)v\otimes D_W(X)w$. If $D_V^a=0$ and $D_W^b=0$, then $P^a=Q^b=0$ and the binomial expansion of $(P+Q)^{a+b}$ is zero, since every term has either at least $a$ factors $P$ or at least $b$ factors $Q$. The commuting-sum and ring-homomorphism clauses of [lem-sfb-nilpotent-exponential-identities], applied also to $T\mapsto T\otimes1$ and $S\mapsto1\otimes S$, give
$$\lambda_{V\otimes W}(X)=E(P+Q)=E(P)E(Q)=(\lambda_V(X)\otimes1)(1\otimes\lambda_W(X))=\lambda_V(X)\otimes\lambda_W(X).$$
The last equality holds on pure tensors, which generate. Thus all three hypotheses of [lem-sfb-affine-group-tensor-reconstruction] have been verified, and it gives a unique $g_X\in G(R)$ acting as $\lambda_V(X)$ in every representation. Applying this to the given representation $i$ gives $i_R(g_X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(\mathrm di_R(X))^j/j!$.

source.place: 14.31 (a) and application of Theorem 9.2, printed p.288.

proof.text: For a $k$-algebra map $\alpha:R\to S$, the matrix of $D_V(X)$ changes coefficientwise to that of $D_V((\alpha\otimes1)X)$. The ring-homomorphism identity of [lem-sfb-nilpotent-exponential-identities] makes the same true of $\lambda_V(X)$. By uniqueness in [lem-sfb-affine-group-tensor-reconstruction], $G(\alpha)(g_X)=g_{(\alpha\otimes1)X}$. To construct an actual morphism, choose a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $\mathfrak g$, put $B=k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]$, and take $X_{\mathrm{univ}}=\sum t_je_j$. The point $g_{X_{\mathrm{univ}}}\in G(B)$ is a $k$-algebra map $k[G]\to B$, hence defines $\exp_G:\operatorname{Spec}B\to G$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Every $X=\sum x_je_j$ is obtained by $t_j\mapsto x_j$, so coefficient naturality shows that this morphism has exactly the points $g_X$. Since $i_R$ is injective (a point is an algebra map from the quotient coordinate ring), the displayed matrix formula characterizes it. For $d=0$ the same construction uses $B=k$ and the zero vector.

source.place: 14.31, printed p.288, naturality in R and passage to a scheme morphism; universal-point construction spelling out the affine Yoneda argument.

proof.text:
The defining equality in every representation, $r_{V,R}(g_X)=E(D_V(X))$, refers only to $G$ and its tangent vector. Repeating the construction using any other closed unitriangular embedding therefore gives the same family and hence the same point by [lem-sfb-affine-group-tensor-reconstruction]; using the universal point gives equality of the morphisms. For a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ and a representation $s$ of $H$, composition on dual-number points gives $\mathrm d(s\circ f)=\mathrm ds\circ\mathrm df$. Thus
$$s_R(f_R(g_X))=E(\mathrm d(s\circ f)_R(X))=E(\mathrm ds_R((1\otimes\mathrm df)(X)))=s_R(\exp_H((1\otimes\mathrm df)(X))).$$
Take $s$ to be the fixed closed unitriangular embedding of $H$ and use its injectivity on $R$-points. This proves the required functoriality for every $R$.

source.place: 14.31, naturality square immediately before Proposition 14.32, printed p.289.

proof.text:
Let $A=\mathrm di_R(X)$ and $B=\mathrm di_R(Y)$ commute. Their sum is $\mathrm di_R(X+Y)$ by linearity of the tangent map; all three are strictly upper triangular and hence nilpotent by step 1. The commuting-sum identity in [lem-sfb-nilpotent-exponential-identities] gives
$$i_R(\exp_G(X+Y))=E(A+B)=E(A)E(B)=i_R(\exp_G(X)\exp_G(Y)).$$
Injectivity of $i_R$ gives the stated equality. This proves only the commuting-sum clause; no inverse to $\exp_G$ is used or constructed. When $n=1$, all tangent matrices are zero and the construction is the identity point.
